extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical Latin poetry (readers of Horace), translators and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading commentary and explanatory notes on Horace's Satires (books II, selected satires), discussing poetic technique, structure, allusion, dating, and textual variants. Intended to guide interpretation, translation, and critical edition work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody / travestying of epic style
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilful parody of epic style shows Horace's satiric power at its best; the travestying of heroic themes is traditional in both satire and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ epic diction and motifs ironically to mock elevated subjects or to deflate heroic pretensions. The commentary cites precedents (Plautus' Amphitryo, Lucilius, Varro, Lucian) and later analogues (Disraeli, Bangs) as models; parody should be recognisable as epic echoes yet inverted in purpose. Avoid mere pastiche — effective parody highlights incongruity between form and subject to produce satiric effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of dramatic form (dialogue vs monologue) suited to tone
rubrics_metrics.description: This satire's peculiarly personal tone leads Horace to abandon a dialogue framework and revert to the monologue form (as in Book I) because the monologue better suits a personal, intimate voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select form to serve tone: use monologue for intimate, confessional, or personal satire; use dialogue when multiple perspectives or a mock-instructional/contest frame is needed. The form should heighten, not undercut, the speaker's stance and rhetorical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural arrangement / structural unity (triptych and contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kiessling notes how morning and evening country-pictures act as side-panels enclosing a central day-in-Rome picture (a triptych); the arrangement artistically presents contrast and is summed up by an allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the poem's macro-structure so that complementary scenes frame the central action, creating thematic resonance. Use parallelism and contrast (e.g., country vs city, morning vs evening) and conclude with an emblematic allegory or fable to unify the work. Good arrangement enhances clarity and aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fable / allegory to encapsulate and close
rubrics_metrics.description: The Satire concludes with the Town and Country Mouse allegory which sums up the contrast between rural peace and urban restlessness; the allegory functions as a delightful, conclusive emblem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a compact allegory or fable at or near the end to crystallise the poem's moral or thematic contrast. The allegory should be apt, recognisable, and rhetorically efficient — not a lengthy digression but a concentrated summary device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-heroic diction and rhetorical apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of certain passages is mock-heroic (mock-heroic diction and apostrophe to gods like Maia/Janus), which serves to heighten the ironic contrast between grand style and humble subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevated diction and classical apostrophes on trivial or domestic topics to produce irony; the incongruity between lofty voice and mundane content produces humour and critique. Maintain enough epic resonance to be perceived as deliberate, otherwise tone collapses into oddity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contemporary/historical allusions for dating and context
rubrics_metrics.description: References (e.g., to Actium, the Dacians, land assignments to veterans) provide evidence for dating composition and situating the poem historically; such allusions are employed in the commentary to infer chronology (composed late 31 B.C. or early 30 B.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed topical or historical references to ground a work in its moment; critics should pay attention to such markers when establishing date or political context. When composing, use topical allusions judiciously — they lend specificity but may require annotation for later readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual echoes and classical exempla
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's lines echo Homeric phrases and recall other classical authors (Menippus, Lucilius, Varro, Lucian). Such echoes place the work in a literary tradition and inform its method (parody, travesty, allusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate intertextual references enrich texture and invite comparison; the writer should be aware of source texts and expectations. Annotators should identify echoes and parallels to illuminate tone, purpose, and lineage. Over-reliance on obscure allusions without cues risks alienating readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal tone and speaker's voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'peculiarly personal tone' of the satire contributes to its charm; first-person narration and anecdotal material make the satire engaging and authentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a consistent speakerly persona when using first person; personal anecdotes can make satiric points vivid and convincing. Maintain a balance so persona does not collapse into mere confession or self-indulgence — the voice should still serve satiric aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory and concrete detail for realism and comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid culinary and domestic details (oils, wines, bowls, smells, fish markets, greasy hands, mould on bowls) give concrete realism and underpin the poem's comic and moral points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory detail to ground satire in everyday life and to generate humour via concrete imagery. Specific, well-chosen details strengthen credibility and the reader's imaginative engagement. Avoid excessive cataloguing that distracts from thematic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and direction of satiric tone (trenchant vs burlesque)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentary calls one poem 'the most trenchant of all the Satires' and notes Horace's 'utmost contempt' for fortune-hunters; choice of severity is a compositional concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how severe the satire should be: trenchant, corrosive attack requires sharper invective and fewer mitigating ironies; lighter burlesque leans on humour and playful inversion. Tone should be consistent enough to be recognisable as intentional but flexible to permit shifts for rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic/mock-instructional frame to satirize conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Art of Legacy-Hunting' is a burlesque set of rules and 'guidelines' that mock the contemporary practice by presenting advice in a didactic mode; the mock-instructional voice satirises unethical behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a pseudo-didactic frame (rules, maxims, step-by-step advice) to expose and ridicule practices by mimicking their rhetoric. Ensure that the instructional voice is plausibly authoritative yet contains signals of irony so readers detect satire rather than genuine counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete anecdote and exemplum
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories and named anecdotes (e.g., the Nasica-Coranus will story, the oiled corpse carried by an heir) are used to illustrate and dramatise satiric points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include compact, memorable anecdotes to embody abstract criticisms — such exempla should be vivid, often comic or grotesque, and directly tied to the larger thematic point. Beware of overlong exempla that overshadow the poem's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual-critical apparatus and editorial transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The edition includes manuscript variants, emendations, and editorial notes (e.g., variant readings, conjectures, marginalia), using them to justify readings and elucidate text and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scholarly editions, supply a clear critical apparatus: list significant manuscript variants, record conjectural emendations, and explain editorial decisions in notes. Provide cultural/historical glosses where needed. Transparency about uncertainty and alternatives is essential for further scholarship.
